p: Yeah. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Yeah. So specifically, the ask would be the cost to taxpayers of processing low-level arrests compared to the cost if those were through issuing summonses or utilizing some other diversion program. So, thank you.

Councilmember, I would– I would say if you are— if we're talking about low-level offenses, the vast majority of the time, if we make an arrest for something that is otherwise summonsable, it will be for one of two reasons. Either we cannot properly identify the person making them ineligible for summons because then the summons means nothing, or there is another warrant that is

outstanding that they haven't responded to for some other crime. I will say that, um, the, the unidentifiable is about 6.6 percent of those, so the vast majority of the time it is– that person is wanted on an open warrant for some other crime. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: So vast majority, can you give a percentage to that? How many of those are— if we're talking– vast majority is well over 50 percent, which I don't know that that's accurate.
Alex can tell you.

So in transit, when we do have to make an arrest, again, it is– as the Commissioner stated it’s 6.6 percent of the time– that's because we were not able to properly identify. The remainder of all the arrests are either because the person has a warrant and we have a legal obligation to bring them back to court, or they're being arrested for a higher-level offense in addition to that low-level. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: You're saying that those are the only two other reasons?
Correct. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay. Can I–
[interposing] Unidentifiable– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Can I follow up on this?
Unidentifiable, wanted on a warrant, and third, being wanted, or—
[interposing] If you are being arrested for a higher-level crime.
In addition to the lower-level crime.
Okay, one more follow-up and then we gotta move on. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Well, it's not one— I have a line of questions, but just responding to that because I have—

Councilmember, we can sit together and– as long as you want and go through any questions that you have on this. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Sure, I know we have— but I actually think that there's a lot of value in not just doing it sitting in a meeting, but doing it in an open hearing with the public so that they know how their money is being spent and what

outcomes they're getting or not getting and what we should be able to expect. I have— I– I'm I will pass it off to you, but I have a second round just specifically on that. Thank you.
Okay. Council Member Wong, followed by Councilmember Ariola.

Okay. Thank you, Chair. And thank you to the Commissioner and the men and women of the NYPD for testifying today. Before my questions, I want to recognize some excellent work by the NYPD. Last week my office with Council Member Ariola's office and community members became aware of social media posts promoting a planned takeover at the Atlas Mall. We immediately shared that information with the NYPD. Queens Borough Chief Russell Greene and Captain Rios took the intelligence seriously and acted quickly, deploying a significant police presence around the mall. For a few hours, the Atlas Mall looked very well secure. That deterrence worked, and the takeover never materialized. When organizers began directing participants towards Middle Village Playground in my district, my office again alerted the NYPD. Officers responded quickly

and prevented any disruption before it could occur. And because of proactive policing, nothing happened. That's exactly what residents expect and deserve. I also want to thank Inspector Wong at the 110th Precinct for his work addressing quality of life concerns, including issues surrounding the Amadeus Nightclub, illegal car meetups, loud music, and other persistent neighborhood complaints. I also want to thank Captain Fennessey of the 112th Precinct for addressing recent antisemitic vandalism affecting the communities in my district and Council Member Schulman's district. I appreciate the work these commanders are doing to keep our neighborhoods safe, address quality of life concerns before they become larger problems, and maintain confidence in public safety. With that, I have a quick— a few questions. Is there a Department policy against publicly disclosing precinct-by-precient staffing levels? And if so, what is the rationale? Because my constituents regularly ask about these figures, and they were— they were— they look and look, and there's nowhere to be published.

So, the way the way the City Council set up the law, you know, we have various disclosure obligations, various— wide range of staffing data that we are required to disclose, except to the extent that it will endanger public safety or endanger our officers. And so we, as you know, we provide a very wide range of data regarding staffing and deployment. However, as it gets more and more granular, more and more specific, we do get more and more concerned about the safety aspect of this. If bad actors know precisely how we have staffed at a very granular level, that allows them to exploit it, to make strategic or tactical decisions that can be incredibly dangerous for the public or for our officers. So that's the balance that we're constantly striking. I do want to emphasize that the City Council set up the law in this way, that is maximum transparency consistent with public safety and the safety of the officers.

Which is why we tend when we talk about publicly about staffing numbers or report publicly on staffing numbers to do it on the borough level. But when you have asked in the past

and other of your colleagues have asked in the past about your staffing numbers, about concerns about staffing, we are very transparent with you in those discussions, take the feedback, and then assign officers accordingly.

Okay, thank you. Recently as the temperature gets warmer, we have a big problem about dirt bikes and ATVs driven on the streets and in parks in my district. Question: is it legal to operate a dirt bike or ATV on a public street or in a park? Even if it's for minors or adults.
An ATV? No, it is not.
What about for dirt bikes? Okay, thank you.
If it's an unregistered dirt bike, no, it cannot. It cannot be on a New York City street.
I see. Oh, thank you. Chair, I would like to have more questions for round two.
Perfect.
Thank you. Thank you.
Thank you. Uh, Council Member Ariola, followed by Council Member Joseph.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Commissioner. Thank you for always coming fully prepared and for testifying with full transparency and clarity. We really do appreciate that. Many of us here want to see the NYPD get more resources than I'm hearing you saying we're getting. So that's what we're here for. As far as numbers, you had them categorized by borough and how crime has decreased by borough, especially retail crimes in specific boroughs. Do you have that drilled down as far as council districts? Because oftentimes we get calls in our council offices that says, oh, it's— we can't even live here anymore, you know, we're ready to go. But we want to be able to tell them, like, you know, I—
Your staffing numbers by council district–
Right? How major–

[interposing] That’s a good idea. I don't think we have that available now, but that would be, I think, high enough level that it wouldn't be at the precinct level. That's actually a really good idea about how to get more granular than just borough.
Right.
And we can try to provide that.

Yeah. So this, this way we can fight back any narrative that says, you know, crime is out of control because I do— I love the Q teams. I love our Community Affairs officers. I agree that we need more heavy toes. I'm so happy that you're open to that, you know, in some of our areas. The other thing is, you said that a lot of your funding comes from federal grants and you're going to continue to fight to get those federal grants, but there is some language that precludes you from being able to apply for those federal grants.
Yes.
And I can only imagine that that includes working fully with federal law enforcement agencies. How–
[interposing] A lot of it is that– a lot of the problematic language for us conflicts with the sanctuary city law.
Correct. So how, how will you manage that, or navigate that when there is a conflict there? Because you certainly need that funding.

So, there's two separate things going on. The first are the grants, which tend to be the much smaller grants. They do not represent a majority of the counterterrorism grant funding we get, where we have that conflict with sanctuary city law, and we are not eligible to apply. The more meaningful chunk of money is not about eligibility— a conflict between sanctuary city law and eligibility requirements. It's the Department of Homeland Security's allocation levels to New York State, which were dramatically cut under Secretary Noem. And we were hopeful that the president would

overrule. Unfortunately, we have not seen those dollars yet for federal fiscal year '25.
Thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Great. Council Member Joseph, followed by Council Member Hanks.
Thank you. Hi, Commissioner. Always good to see you. I'm right here.
Hello.

Hello. Correct me if I'm wrong. Youth arrests for major felonies have increased in each of the last fiscal years, at the same time major felony crimes in schools relatively flat over the period. How can we improve those stats? You know how I feel about that. And what other agencies and programs can NYPD reach, I believe, would be great partners?
Hold on, I have two people— he's explaining to me the first part of your question. Okay, sorry, what's the second part of the question?

How are you working with other agencies to make sure we're

bringing down the numbers among young people that we're seeing in these cases?
Alex is gonna answer the first part of the question since–
After he explained the question, all right.
he was just [inaudible].

So I can answer the first part. Sorry, there's lots of different things going on at once. All right. So, arrests in schools are actually down. So this year they're down 4.8 percent. So we're seeing both less crime and less less arrests in schools at the same time.

But how are– are you also working in collaboration with schools? For example, I knew before there was a division working on school– there was a drone for subway surfing. We lost a young person at 14 years old to subway surfing. The last hearing that I had here with Transportation, NYPD, and New York City Public Schools as interagency— these are conversations that

all agencies should be having. So where are we on that in terms of collaboration and working on all of things?

Collaboration with DOE, I hope if you ask them, they will say the same thing. But from our perspective, the collaboration with DOE specifically has never been better. I'll let Tania speak about the work that we're doing with DOE, and then I want to speak a little bit about the work that we're doing with them with subway surfing. Go ahead.
Okay.
How you doing?
I'm good.
So we take arrests– we work with our DOE partners really well.
You facilitated that whole thing?
Yes.
You had the first meeting?

Yes. 65% of incidents that occur in schools now are mitigated by DOE. We meet with our DOE partners on a monthly basis. We also meet with the advocates on a quarterly basis to try to work with the advocates in DOE too, so we don't have to arrest and have DOE take on more of the incidents.
So you're working interagency, so you're working with Project Pivot, who's on the ground–
Yes.
which is the cure violence groups they have in schools.
Yes, 351 schools Project Pivot is in. We provide support in those schools during the times that Project Pivot is going on.
Okay, in your crisis intervention team training, the numbers that was for uniform members in communication skills, de-escalation, and behavior and restorative justice, of course.
So we have approximately 3,384 personnel trained.
In de-escalation–
[interposing] Yes.
restorative justice. We received a couple of calls around your metal detectors are not working at schools and students are being late. How are you addressing that?

So we know of three incidents that occurred this year thus far, but the school safety executive leadership responded and spoke to all three principals. We have now have an in-house training of our agents to help mitigate if a scanner breaks. Within 30 minutes, we have agents rectifying the issue. And as well as now there's a direct notification and investigation done once we are aware that a school is late because of scanning issues or personnel issues.

Based on the feedback that you've given me about this specific thing in the past, I am pleased to tell you that we have ordered 40 new scanners to replace some of the old equipment

that we have, because it is not acceptable to be late for school because of scanning.
And we received 10 of those scanners on Friday, last Friday.
Okay, good. And they will— what's the timeline to put them in place for them, or are they already in place?
We're working on that now with DOE. We're working with Mark and our executives in school safety to procure where exactly they're going to go or replace.
This council had passed the bill for 988 to be in New York City public schools. How many calls do you get from young people? Can— do you track that?
We would not have that data. That data, you need to ask 988, the people who run that, because all we do is transfer the call, so we don't collect the demographic information.

And how many mental health-related calls where this training would

be applicable if you were to do it? You can get back to me on that.
Mental health-related 911 calls?
Yes.

We can get you the number of mental health 911 calls. I know that in the first 15 days, 204 calls were transferred to 988, but that is nowhere near the total number. You're asking for the total number of any EDP call we get.

And as my colleague had mentioned earlier, it'd be great to look at the breakdowns per council district in order for us to work better with you, probably provide more resources and provide more support.
We will get that to you.
Thank you. Chair, I'll come around my second round.

Thank you. Thank you so much, Council Member Joseph. So it is 12:10. We're gonna take a brief five-minute recess. 12:10, so we'll see everybody at 12:15. Thank you so much. And

please, just five minutes. It is 12:10. I'll see everybody at 12:15. Thank you. [break]
Everyone please find your seats. We’re getting ready to resume the hearing. Thank you. Please find your seats.
Okay, great. Okay. So we're going to resume with Council Member Hanks and then Council Member Brooks-Powers.

Thank you, Chair. It's good to see you, everyone, Commissioner Tish. So I'd just like to circle back to the Office of Community Safety. And just for the record, can we kind of— whatever, you know, give a list of existing programs under OCS if they're— if there is—
I do not have that list.

Oh, you don't have the list? Okay. So, as a holistic structure, it's still, you know, quite vague what this is. Does NYPD have any idea of what they would want to partner with or need support with or any gaps that would help define this OCS committee group?

As I mentioned, we do a tremendous amount of work with a lot of the offices that have been moved under OCS. The Office to End Gender-Based Violence is a shining example of that partnership, and that work continues. Look, I think the mental health crisis in New York City is definitely an issue that affects the New York City Police Department profoundly. And so I would look forward to walking— working with the Office of Community Safety to understand ideas that they have for addressing it.

Thank you so much. I'll have a line of questioning that's a bit more local. So, the Borough Patrol Staten Island is funded at $103.2 million in the FY 27 Executive Plan, down by $7.9 million from the $111 million FY 26 adopted level. Primarily in the 20th precinct headquarters at 78 Richmond Terrace in St. George, with parts in the 121st. Why does the Borough Patrol Staten Island fall $7.9 million below FY 26 adopted level in the Executive Plan, and what does it mean for authorized officer counts at the 120 and the 121 precincts?

So, as I mentioned, we did reorganization of department resources last year to better— to streamline, for example, our response to domestic violence, and also to make our evidence collection teams work more closely with our Crime Scene Unit. And so in doing that, we moved those two units from under the Patrol Services Bureau to the Detective Bureau. Those movements happened across the entire Department, and they certainly did not take resources away from community members. It just looks on paper like we've taken resources out of patrol, but those functions still remain just assigned under a different command code.
Thank you so much. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you. Council Member Brooks-Powers?

Thank you, and thank you, Commissioner. I first want to thank you Patrick Gordon, Ryan, for bringing the team back out when we unfortunately lost 18-year-old Brandon Figueroa at sea in Rockaway. It was meaningful. The mother was definitely appreciative. I'm hopeful that

the body that came ashore yesterday is Brandon's body, but we know that PD is still maintaining regular communication with us. So thank you for that.
Absolutely.

I also want to thank Chief Obe and her division for the work that they've been doing, including Officer Marian Manick [sp?], who has been amazing since your visit to Southeast Queens regarding the illegal truck parking in Southeast Queens. It has been tremendous. So thank you for that.
Great. That makes me so happy to hear.

And then I'm going to just ask you three questions. If I need to repeat anything, let me know. So first, Southeast Queens has seen a surge in gun violence in the last few months, including the tragic shooting of 15-year-old Jaden Pierre in the Deputy Speaker's District, which is a neighboring district to mine. As summer approaches and our youth are out of school, how is NYPD prepared to prevent these types of tragic shootings from happening in the first place? Often

these violent outbursts are the result of organized takeovers that spread on social media. I'm curious to know how the NYPD is detecting these social media trends and getting ahead of potentially violent incidents and how NYPD is communicating to the local precincts when viral social media trends pop up in specific geographies. Then—
[interposing] Sorry, I'm not smart enough to remember all of these. Can we do them one at a time?
Well, because of the interest of time—
Okay, okay. Say that–
[interposing] I'll repeat whatever I need to.
Yeah.

So from the end of December 24 to October 25, NYC admitted on average 49 more people to jail each month than at discharge, increasing the jail population by around 500 people. As we approach the transition to borough-based jails, our city must work to reduce the

incarcerated population. I wanted to know how NYPD specifically is working with Department of Corrections, MOCJ, the DAs, and other agencies to work towards a common ground and ensure we can successfully close Rikers. So, just wanting to know that coordination is happening there. And lastly, we have consistently heard from community members and local precincts that police officers are not aware of local laws regarding the truck routes, truck idling, and other park-related– trucking-related matters. The result is that there are no— there is no consistent enforcement against trucks breaking the laws. What steps has NYPD taken to ensure that all police officers are trained on this issue and able to enforce traffic laws against trucks that are not compliant? And I'll give you an example. We did a walkthrough with DOT, and there was a truck that was idling on Springfield Boulevard, and we had a local officer there as well. But it was clear that it was not clear in terms of how long that truck was able to legally idle in that location?
Okay, I'll start with that one first, and then you have to remind me about the other one.
Sorry.

The— if there is a precinct where we have to do specific refresher training on specific laws like truck idling laws, we are very happy to do that and to do that quickly. So my team can connect with you to understand, like, what the very specific issue is. And you have my commitment that those officers in that command will be refreshed in those issues. You asked, I think, your second to last question— I'm working backwards here— was about Rikers. And I'll just be– be blunt. The NYPD does not think in terms of the size of the correction population or the Rikers population. That is a matter specifically for the Department of Correction. We don't enjoy arresting people, but we need— we will take action when there is a crime committed. And so my hope and my expectation is that the city will account for that in their planning for correction capacity.

And just to clarify, because I think we're in alignment and not necessarily wanting people who should be in custody to be in custody, it's more in terms of looking at that— the low-level offenses that I think you mentioned earlier that could be a summons, for example, but understanding that coordination because we are seeing an increase in the arrests that are happening and we're not seeing that revolving door for those that may be instances where there could be summonses or low-level in a sense.

So we, we allow our officers to use discretion. Where you are seeing increased increases in arrests– like, where you're seeing arrests for something that would otherwise be some summonsable, is generally in three areas. One, the person cannot be properly identified, which is out of the officer's control. If the person cannot provide ID or the Department cannot properly identify them, they are not eligible for a summons. Doesn't matter how low the offense is. And if they are able to provide it, oftentimes they are. Second is if they are wanted on an open warrant that they themselves

have not responded to and are required by law to respond to and we are— we come across them for a low-level thing, we will arrest them and return them to— they need to be returned to court to deal with that open warrant. So I just don't want there– I reject the narrative that the NYPD is on a spree of arresting people for low-level offenses when the actual data shows otherwise.

Thank you. And just going back to the first one, it was more centered around the takeover overs in the social media efforts that I know PD has technology and they are viewing different social medias to try to stay up to speed with what's happening with the young people, but wanting to know what that coordination with the local precinct looks like so that we can be more proactive in responding to it.

The Chief is going to take this one, but I just want to say social media is driving right now two big things that I know are of particular concern to many of you here, car meets and teen takeovers, which are exploding and I– across the country, and I expect only to get more intense as

school lets out. We have— we monitor social media for both of those things, but your question is specifically about teen takeovers, and the Chief will–
[interposing] Yes.
let you know how we approach those and how we coordinate with the local precincts on them.

Good afternoon. So actually, the local precinct is the first line of defense when it comes to monitoring social media. We have field intelligence officers assigned to all 78 precincts across New York City, our housing PSAs, and also our transit, our transit PAs. We do have a centralized social media team out of our Detective Bureau, but also out of our Intelligence Bureau. But it starts with the local precinct. So if a field intelligence officer is monitoring social media in the 101 in Far Rockaway, he or she, through our ECMS system will share that intelligence, not just locally, but citywide. And we, you know, again, we're very good at knowing the platforms that we need to

look at, but that's real time. Like, that's real time. We don't wait. That gets sent out immediately and everybody is always working together. And we've gotten very, very good with the car meets and also the teen takeovers with sharing that intelligence, right? One of the four principles of– actually two out of the four principles of CompStat is timely and accurate intelligence and rapid deployment. And that's a staple of the New York City Police Department.

And I just want to add on your last question– I'm sorry, I lost the forest through the trees, threw me off for a second. Low-level arrests don't end up in Rikers. You end up in Rikers for a felony. So I— low-level arrests are not driving the Rikers population.

So not everyone at Rikers are there for a felony. I know Council Member Cabán is going to probably dig more into this later, so I'm not going to take up more of the committee's time on it. I do want to thank you for your responses and just make a plug for the 101 Precinct in terms of capital needs, because that

precinct right now is highly dilapidated and under-resourced as well. But thank you, Chairs.
Thank you. Okay, we have Council Member Felder. Council Member Felder versus Council Member— and next we have Council Member Brewer followed by Rustler. Okay, Council Member Felder, go ahead.

I apologize because I'm going to be leaving for implant, not in the brain, in the tooth— teeth. So, I'm sorry, but I don't want you to answer my questions first, but if somebody could call or let me know afterwards, I'd be very happy. So, first of all, I want to thank your colleague here who spent hours at the hearings on antisemitism, listening to questions and answering them. I've never ever been at a hearing when someone didn't say once, in my— at least when I was awake, didn't say once, I'll get back to you. He answered—
[interposing] He’s fabulous.
He answered every single question.
Fabulous. I never saw that in my life.
That’s what we try to do. We try to answer your questions.

I never saw that in my life. I think there's something wrong with him. I think you should check it out. Yeah, okay. In terms of my questions, if you could just— if somebody could let me know. Number one, I'd like to know in terms of the community policing, if somebody could let me know if there's a particular person that's assigned to the district. I don't know how exactly it works. I'd like to know who that person is so that I could call.
We'll get you in touch with the community affairs officers in your precincts.
Yeah, if somebody could— yeah, that would— yeah. But I asked you not to answer my question.
Oh, sorry, I missed that.

Yeah, so if you could please listen— yeah, please. The other thing is

that for years ago, they used to have a program where they had officers, for example, that looked— not great, but looked like me, for example, policing, you know, were– are actually cops walking around that looked like Orthodox Jews. And, you know, the— I think that the concept, when they publicized it, that alone was helpful. I'm curious why that has not been used in terms of fighting antisemitism. That's two. Three, there– years ago, I don't know how many, I think it's about 15 years ago, they installed certain cameras on top of the lights to fight crime. I don't know if those cameras are operational or not. And finally, when I was in the Senate about four years– five years ago, I sponsored a bill to actually have insurance and licenses and other things, you know, on bicycles, certain bicycles, even regular bicycles. And I've seen some talk about it, and I'd like to know what the– you know, whether the Police Department, you know, has any opinions on it. And I thank you very, very much for everything that you're doing, period.
Thank you so much, Council Member. At your request, we will get back to you in writing on all of those things.
I thank you.
But I don't want that held against us in terms of our live response rate for this hearing. 'Cause I could have answered all of them right here and now.
I'm not listening to you because I make the jokes. You are not— it's my show, you know.
